props.title: The Landlord
props.initialSlug: White man buys tenement, upends lives & himself

sections.content: **The Landlord (1970)** (1970) marks Hal Ashby's directorial debut and stands as a pioneering examination of race, gentrification, and privilege in American cinema. Coming at the tail end of the Civil Rights era, it follows a wealthy white man buying a Brooklyn tenement with plans to evict Black residents and create his dream home. The film's biting satire predates later gentrification narratives like Do the Right Thing (1989) by nearly two decades. Beau Bridges delivers a transformative performance as Elgar, while Diana Sands and Pearl Bailey bring depth and humanity to roles that could have been stereotypes in lesser hands.

sections.content: Ashby went on to define the 1970s counterculture with films like Harold and Maude (1971) and **Coming Home** (1978), but The Landlord's fearless tackling of race relations and class privilege set the template for his career-long focus on outsiders and social issues. The film's innovative mix of comedy and serious drama influenced later works like **Sorry to Bother You** (2018) and **Get Out** (2017), which similarly use genre-bending approaches to explore racial dynamics.

Screenwriter Bill Gunn, who also directed the experimental vampire film Ganja & Hess (1973), brings a complex understanding of racial politics that was rare for Hollywood in 1970. The film's exploration of white privilege and unconscious bias feels startlingly contemporary, predating contemporary discussions by decades. Like **Shadows** (1959) by John Cassavetes, it captures a raw, unvarnished view of race relations that mainstream cinema rarely touched. SUBHEAD: New Hollywood's Social Conscience

sections.content: The Landlord emerged during a crucial shift in American cinema, alongside films like **Medium Cool** (1969) and **The Learning Tree** (1969) that brought documentary-like realism to discussions of social issues. Gordon Parks Jr. would follow a similar path with **Super Fly** (1972), using genre conventions to explore urban life while avoiding exploitation. Ashby's film stands out for addressing gentrification decades before it became a widespread concern, seen in later films like **Last Black Man in San Francisco** (2019).
